---
title: "Medicare at 65: Sharp RD Estimates"
subtitle: "The effect of Medicare eligibility on healthcare use, with robustness checks"
knit: |
  (function(inputFile, ...) {
    candidates <- c(
      file.path(Sys.getenv('LOCALAPPDATA'), 'Programs', 'Pandoc'),
      file.path(Sys.getenv('LOCALAPPDATA'), 'Pandoc'),
      file.path(Sys.getenv('ProgramFiles'), 'Pandoc'),
      file.path(Sys.getenv('ProgramFiles'), 'RStudio', 'resources',
                'app', 'bin', 'quarto', 'bin', 'tools')
    )
    found <- candidates[file.exists(file.path(candidates, 'pandoc.exe'))]
    if (length(found)) Sys.setenv(RSTUDIO_PANDOC = found[1])
    project <- dirname(normalizePath(inputFile, winslash = '/', mustWork = TRUE))
    while (!file.exists(file.path(project, 'data', 'nhis_clean_full.csv'))) {
      parent <- dirname(project)
      if (identical(parent, project)) stop('Cannot locate project data.')
      project <- parent
    }
    destination <- file.path(project, 'output', 'sharp_rd_estimation')
    dir.create(destination, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
    options <- list(...)
    options$output_dir <- destination
    options$intermediates_dir <- tempdir()
    do.call(rmarkdown::render, c(list(input = inputFile), options))
  })
output:
  html_document:
    toc: true
    toc_float: true
    toc_depth: 2
    number_sections: true
    theme: flatly
    highlight: tango
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo=FALSE,message=FALSE,error=FALSE,
                      fig.width=9,fig.height=5,dpi=160,fig.align='center')
source('rd_functions.R')
root <- find_root()
out <- file.path(root,'output','sharp_rd_estimation')
dir.create(out,recursive=TRUE,showWarnings=FALSE)
d <- load_rd_data(root)
stopifnot(all(is.na(d$group[is.na(d$lowed_clean)])))
H <- 5; H_alt <- c(3,4,5,6,7)
outcomes <- c('sawdr','inhosp')
covars <- c('female','bnh','hispanic','onh','lowed_clean','region_1','region_2','region_3')
pv <- function(p) format.pval(p,digits=3,eps=.001)
ci <- function(r) sprintf('[%s, %s]',pct(r$ci_lower),pct(r$ci_upper))
```

```{r estimates, include=FALSE}
run <- function(y,check,spec,data=d,...) cbind(check=check,spec=spec,fit_rd(data,y,...)$row)
d_cov <- d[complete.cases(d[,covars]),]
below <- subset(d,age4<65)
above <- subset(d,age4>=65.25)
full <- subset(d,!(age4>=65 & age4<66))
est <- do.call(rbind,lapply(outcomes,function(y) rbind(
  run(y,'main','Main: +/-5 years',h=H),
  do.call(rbind,lapply(setdiff(H_alt,H),function(h) run(y,'bandwidth',paste0('+/-',h,' years'),h=h))),
  run(y,'functional form','Local quadratic, +/-5 years',h=H,poly=2),
  run(y,'covariates','No covariates, covariate sample',data=d_cov,h=H),
  run(y,'covariates','With covariates',data=d_cov,h=H,covars=covars),
  run(y,'donut','Donut: drop 65.00',h=H,donut=.25),
  run(y,'donut','Donut: drop 64.75-65.25',h=H,donut=.5),
  run(y,'exposure exclusion','Exclude ages 65.00-65.75',data=full,h=H),
  run(y,'placebo','Placebo at 63',data=below,h=2,cutoff=63),
  run(y,'placebo','Placebo at 64',data=below,h=2,cutoff=64),
  run(y,'placebo','Placebo at 66',data=above,h=2,cutoff=66),
  run(y,'placebo','Placebo at 67',data=above,h=2,cutoff=67))))
est$label <- unname(rd_labels[est$outcome])
main <- subset(est,check=='main')
main$p_holm <- p.adjust(main$p_value,'holm')
m1 <- main[main$outcome=='sawdr',]; m2 <- main[main$outcome=='inhosp',]
tab <- function(checks,with_main=FALSE) {
  z <- subset(est,check %in% c(checks,if(with_main) 'main'))
  z <- z[order(match(z$outcome,outcomes)),]
  table_rd(z,paste0(z$label,': ',z$spec))
}
```

```{r sensitivity-inputs, include=FALSE}
wmean <- function(y,w) {
  ok <- is.finite(y) & is.finite(w) & w>0
  weighted.mean(y[ok],w[ok])
}
e <- fit_rd(d,'emp',H)$row
c62 <- fit_rd(d,'emp',2,62)$row
pre <- subset(d,age4>=60 & age4<65)
bound <- do.call(rbind,lapply(outcomes,function(y) {
  gap <- wmean(pre[[y]][pre$emp %in% 0],pre$wt[pre$emp %in% 0])-
         wmean(pre[[y]][pre$emp %in% 1],pre$wt[pre$emp %in% 1])
  data.frame(outcome=y,max_bias=max(0,-e$ci_lower)*abs(gap))
}))
sub <- do.call(rbind,lapply(1:4,function(g) {
  dg <- subset(d,group==g); pg <- subset(dg,age4>=60 & age4<65)
  data.frame(group=g,label=group_labels[[as.character(g)]],
    mcare_jump=fit_rd(dg,'mcare',H)$row$estimate,
    emp_jump=fit_rd(dg,'emp',H)$row$estimate,
    pre_uninsured=1-wmean(pg$covered2,pg$wt))
}))
```

# Specification

## Estimand

We estimate the jump in healthcare use at age 65:

$$\tau_{RD}=\lim_{a\downarrow 65}E[Y_i\mid Age_i=a]-\lim_{a\uparrow 65}E[Y_i\mid Age_i=a].$$

Treatment is **eligibility**, $1(Age_i\ge65)$, so under the identifying assumptions $\tau_{RD}$ is the local intention-to-treat effect of becoming eligible for Medicare for people near 65. It is not an enrollment effect. A fuzzy RD would estimate a local enrollment effect for compliers under additional first-stage, exclusion and monotonicity assumptions. The main outcome is seeing a doctor in the past year (`sawdr`). An overnight hospital stay in the past year (`inhosp`) is secondary.

## Estimator

Local linear regression within **`r H` years of 65**, with separate age slopes on each side, survey-year fixed effects, NHIS survey weights and a triangular kernel. Standard errors are heteroskedasticity-robust (HC1). The specification is identical to the identification report; both use `rd_functions.R`.

$$Y_i=\alpha+\tau\,1(Age_i\ge65)+\beta(Age_i-65)+\delta\,1(Age_i\ge65)(Age_i-65)+\lambda_{year(i)}+\varepsilon_i,\qquad |Age_i-65|<`r H`.$$

The sample is `r format(nrow(d),big.mark=',')` respondents from NHIS `r min(d$year)`-`r max(d$year)`, of whom `r format(m1$n_left+m1$n_right,big.mark=',')` are within `r H` years of 65.

## Identification evidence

The identification diagnostics provide supporting evidence about local comparability, not proof of continuity. The employment jump at 65 is `r pct(e$estimate)` pp (95% CI `r ci(e)`; p = `r pv(e$p_value)`). At 62 it is `r pct(c62$estimate)` pp (p = `r pv(c62$p_value)`). A detected change at 62 does not establish equal power at 65. Quarter-age coding may misclassify eligibility near the threshold, and both outcomes include the preceding 12 months. Donut specifications assess sensitivity to these features without resolving them completely.

# Graphical evidence

```{r outcome-plots, fig.width=10, fig.height=4.8, fig.cap='Healthcare use around age 65. Points are survey-weighted quarter-age means; lines are local linear fits within five years of 65.'}
par(mfrow=c(1,2),mar=c(4,4.5,3,1))
for(y in outcomes) plot_rd(d,y,H)
par(mfrow=c(1,1))
```

Each point is the share of respondents in one quarter-year age cell who saw a doctor (left) or had a hospital stay (right) in the past year. The blue line is fitted to ages below 65 and the orange line to ages 65 and above. The vertical gap between the lines at 65 is the estimated discontinuity.

# Main estimates

```{r main-table, results='asis'}
cat(table_rd(main,main$label),sep='\n')
```

The table reports unadjusted p-values and Holm-adjusted p-values across the two main outcome tests. Doctor visits remain the prespecified primary outcome and hospital stays secondary. Adjusted p-values are `r pv(m1$p_holm)` and `r pv(m2$p_holm)`, respectively; these do not adjust all robustness or subgroup tests.

<div class="finding">

**Doctor visits.** The estimated age-65 discontinuity in the probability of having seen a doctor is **`r pct(m1$estimate)` percentage points** (95% CI `r ci(m1)`; p = `r pv(m1$p_value)`). Just below 65, `r pct(m1$below_rate,1)`% of people saw a doctor, so this is a relative change of `r pct(m1$relative,1)`%. `r if(m1$p_value<.05) 'The jump is statistically significant at 5%.' else 'The confidence interval includes zero, so the jump is not statistically significant at 5%. This does not establish a zero effect.'`

**Hospital stays.** The probability of an overnight hospital stay changes by **`r pct(m2$estimate)` pp** (95% CI `r ci(m2)`; p = `r pv(m2$p_value)`), against `r pct(m2$below_rate,1)`% just below 65, a relative change of `r pct(m2$relative,1)`%. `r if(m2$p_value<.05) 'The jump is statistically significant at 5%.' else 'The jump is not statistically significant at 5%.'`

</div>

# Retirement sensitivity

As an illustrative scenario, we multiply the negative endpoint of the employment confidence interval (or zero if positive) by the absolute utilisation gap between non-workers and workers aged 60-64.75. This assumes that net employment changes capture the relevant retirement response and that the observed utilisation gap is an appropriate effect size. Neither assumption is established: non-employment is not equivalent to retirement, offsetting flows can conceal retirement, and health selection affects the gap. This calculation is not a causal upper bound and omits uncertainty in the utilisation gap.

```{r bias-compare}
bc <- merge(bound,main[,c('outcome','estimate')],by='outcome')
bc <- bc[match(outcomes,bc$outcome),]
bc$share <- ifelse(abs(bc$estimate)>1e-8,bc$max_bias/abs(bc$estimate),NA_real_)
```

```{r bias-table, results='asis'}
cat(knitr::kable(data.frame(Outcome=unname(rd_labels[bc$outcome]),
  `Estimated jump (pp)`=pct(bc$estimate),
  `Scenario magnitude (pp)`=pct(bc$max_bias),
  `Scenario / absolute jump`=paste0(pct(bc$share,1),'%'),check.names=FALSE),
  align='lrrr',row.names=FALSE),sep='\n')
```

The scenario magnitude is **`r pct(bc$max_bias[1])` pp for doctor visits** and
**`r pct(bc$max_bias[2])` pp for hospital stays**. These comparisons neither rule out larger retirement effects nor provide adjusted causal estimates. Ratios to small or imprecisely estimated outcome jumps should be interpreted cautiously.

# Robustness of the estimates

These checks show sensitivity to bandwidth, functional form, controls and sample exclusions. Stability is useful evidence but does not establish a causal interpretation.

## Bandwidth

```{r bandwidth-table, results='asis'}
cat(tab('bandwidth',with_main=TRUE),sep='\n')
```

Narrow windows compare people closer to 65 but use fewer observations, so they are noisier. Wide windows are more precise but rely more on the straight-line approximation.

## Functional form

```{r quadratic-table, results='asis'}
cat(tab('functional form',with_main=TRUE),sep='\n')
```

A straight line on each side could mistake curvature in the age profile for a jump. A local quadratic allows for curvature, at the cost of precision with so few distinct age values.

## Covariate adjustment

Covariate adjustment checks sensitivity to sex, race/ethnicity, education and region. Education is missing for some respondents, so both rows use the same reduced sample; their difference reflects adjustment rather than sample composition. Small changes are consistent with stability, but do not establish balance or repair a discontinuous confounder.

```{r covariate-table, results='asis'}
cat(tab('covariates'),sep='\n')
```

## Donut RD

```{r donut-table, results='asis'}
cat(tab('donut',with_main=TRUE),sep='\n')
```

- **Drop 65.00.** The quarter-age measure may mix actual eligibility states around the birthday. Dropping this cell checks sensitivity to that coding; the direction of the resulting change is not predetermined.
- **Drop 64.75-65.25.** If people postpone care until they are covered, use dips just before 65 and rebounds just after, which would inflate the jump. Dropping these cells checks sensitivity to local timing and anticipation but does not eliminate either concern. The nearest retained cells are 64.50 and 65.50, so the fit extrapolates across a one-year separation.

## Excluding the first year after eligibility

Both outcomes refer to the past 12 months. Respondents just above 65 report utilisation that partly occurred before eligibility, so the age-65 discontinuity does not measure a full year of post-eligibility utilisation. A gradual response may appear in the age slope rather than a level jump; attenuation is not guaranteed.

Dropping ages 65.00-65.75 leaves the right-hand fit starting at recorded age 66. Its prediction at 65 is an extrapolation, not a directly observed full-year treatment effect. This is an additional specification check, not an alternative estimate of the same local effect with assured bias reduction.

```{r full-table, results='asis'}
cat(tab('exposure exclusion',with_main=TRUE),sep='\n')
```

```{r full-compare, include=FALSE}
fe <- subset(est,check=='exposure exclusion'); fe <- fe[match(outcomes,fe$outcome),]
```

The extrapolated jump is `r pct(fe$estimate[1])` pp for doctor visits
(95% CI `r ci(fe[1,])`) and `r pct(fe$estimate[2])` pp for hospital stays
(95% CI `r ci(fe[2,])`). Differences from the main specification may reflect exposure timing, curvature or extrapolation error.

## Placebo cutoffs

If the method picks up noise or curvature, it would find "jumps" at ages where nothing changes. Each placebo uses a two-year window and data from one side of 65 only, so the real jump cannot leak in: cutoffs at 63 and 64 use ages up to 64.75; cutoffs at 66 and 67 use ages from 65.25.

```{r placebo-table, results='asis'}
cat(tab('placebo'),sep='\n')
```

<div class="caution">

Placebo results need not be zero if there is anticipation, another age-related change, or misspecification of the local age trend. At 64 and 66, the windows are asymmetric because observations are restricted to one side of 65. A significant estimate is a reason to investigate, rather than evidence of a specific mechanism or a result to dismiss automatically.

</div>

```{r placebo-summary, include=FALSE}
pl <- subset(est,check=='placebo')
pl_sig <- pl[pl$p_value<.05,]
```

`r if(nrow(pl_sig)==0) 'No placebo cutoff shows a significant jump for either outcome.' else paste0(nrow(pl_sig),' of ',nrow(pl),' placebo estimates are significant at 5%: ',paste(paste0(pl_sig$label,' at ',pl_sig$cutoff,' (',pct(pl_sig$estimate),' pp)'),collapse='; '),'. With ',nrow(pl),' tests, about ',round(.05*nrow(pl),1),' would be significant by chance alone; see the caution above for cutoffs 64 and 66.')`

## All specifications

```{r forest, fig.width=10, fig.height=6.5, fig.cap='Every estimate with its 95% confidence interval. Teal: estimates of the jump at 65. Orange: placebo cutoffs, where the true jump should be zero. The dotted line marks the main estimate.'}
specs <- unique(est$spec)
par(mfrow=c(1,2),mar=c(4,1,3,1),oma=c(0,15,0,0))
for(y in outcomes) {
  z <- est[est$outcome==y,][match(specs,est$spec[est$outcome==y]),]
  yy <- rev(seq_along(specs)); col <- ifelse(z$check=='placebo','#c17948','#176d85')
  plot(100*z$estimate,yy,xlim=range(0,100*c(z$ci_lower,z$ci_upper)),ylim=c(.5,length(specs)+.5),
       yaxt='n',pch=19,col=col,xlab='Jump (pp)',ylab='',main=rd_labels[y],bty='l',
       col.main='#17465c',col.axis='#637783')
  abline(v=0,lty=2,col='#82949f'); abline(v=100*z$estimate[z$check=='main'],lty=3,col='#176d85')
  abline(h=sum(z$check=='placebo')+.5,col='#dde7eb')
  segments(100*z$ci_lower,yy,100*z$ci_upper,yy,col=col,lwd=2)
  if(y==outcomes[1]) axis(2,at=yy,labels=specs,las=1,cex.axis=.85,col.axis='#344f60',outer=TRUE,line=-1)
}
par(mfrow=c(1,1),oma=c(0,0,0,0))
```

# Subgroup comparisons

We compare four race-by-education groups. Groups are reconstructed from White non-Hispanic status and the cleaned below-high-school indicator; respondents with missing education are excluded from subgroup analysis, rather than assigned to low education. Coverage and employment comparisons are re-estimated on these corrected groups in this report, avoiding dependence on older subgroup exports. The main pooled estimates retain respondents with missing education.

Larger coverage jumps could accompany larger utilisation jumps if effects per induced enrollee were similar across groups. However, treatment-effect heterogeneity, insurance generosity and retirement responses can break this ranking. The four-group patterns are descriptive and do not isolate a causal mechanism.

```{r subgroups}
sg <- do.call(rbind,lapply(outcomes,function(y) do.call(rbind,lapply(sub$group,function(g) {
  r <- fit_rd(subset(d,group==g),y,H)$row
  data.frame(outcome=y,group=g,est=r$estimate,se=r$se,lo=r$ci_lower,hi=r$ci_upper,p=r$p_value,below=r$below_rate)
}))))
sg <- merge(sg,sub[,c('group','label','mcare_jump','pre_uninsured','emp_jump')],by='group')
sg <- sg[order(match(sg$outcome,outcomes),sg$group),]
agree <- do.call(rbind,lapply(outcomes,function(y) {
  z <- sg[sg$outcome==y,]
  a <- z[z$group==1,]; b <- z[z$group==4,]
  diff <- b$est-a$est; se <- sqrt(a$se^2+b$se^2)
  data.frame(outcome=y,
    rho_mcare=cor(z$est,z$mcare_jump,method='spearman'),
    rho_uninsured=cor(z$est,z$pre_uninsured,method='spearman'),
    rho_emp=cor(z$est,-z$emp_jump,method='spearman'),
    diff=diff,diff_lo=diff-1.96*se,diff_hi=diff+1.96*se,diff_p=2*pnorm(-abs(diff/se)))
}))
```

## Outcome jumps by group

```{r subgroup-table, results='asis'}
cat(knitr::kable(data.frame(Outcome=unname(rd_labels[sg$outcome]),Group=sg$label,
  `Outcome jump (pp)`=sprintf('%s [%s, %s]',pct(sg$est),pct(sg$lo),pct(sg$hi)),
  `p-value`=pv(sg$p),
  `Medicare jump (pp)`=pct(sg$mcare_jump,1),
  `Uninsured before 65`=paste0(pct(sg$pre_uninsured,1),'%'),
  `Employment jump (pp)`=pct(sg$emp_jump,1),check.names=FALSE),
  align='llrrrrr',row.names=FALSE),sep='\n')
```

```{r subgroup-plot, fig.width=10, fig.height=9, fig.cap='Outcome jumps by group (with 95% confidence intervals) against the Medicare coverage jump (left) and the share uninsured before 65 (right). If outcome jumps follow one of the two measures, the points rise from left to right in that panel.'}
short <- c('1'='White high-ed','2'='White low-ed','3'='Minority high-ed','4'='Minority low-ed')
scatter <- function(z,x,xlab,main) {
  plot(100*x,100*z$est,ylim=range(0,100*c(z$lo,z$hi)),xlim=range(100*x)+c(-3,3),pch=19,col='#176d85',
       xlab=xlab,ylab='Outcome jump at 65 (pp)',main=main,bty='l',col.main='#17465c',col.axis='#637783')
  abline(h=0,lty=2,col='#82949f')
  segments(100*x,100*z$lo,100*x,100*z$hi,col='#176d85',lwd=2)
  text(100*x,100*z$est,short[as.character(z$group)],pos=4,cex=.8,col='#344f60')
}
par(mfrow=c(2,2),mar=c(4.5,4.5,3,1))
for(y in outcomes) {
  z <- sg[sg$outcome==y,]
  scatter(z,z$mcare_jump,'Medicare coverage jump at 65 (pp)',rd_labels[y])
  scatter(z,z$pre_uninsured,'Uninsured before 65 (%)',rd_labels[y])
}
par(mfrow=c(1,1))
```

## Comparison of subgroup patterns

The rank correlations below describe how closely the ordering of outcome jumps matches each measure, from -1 (reversed) to 1 (identical). With four groups they are descriptive, not tests. An exploratory contrast compares White high-education and minority low-education respondents. Its standard error treats the disjoint groups as independent, consistent with the report's observation-level HC1 approximation; it does not account for NHIS design dependence.

```{r agree-table, results='asis'}
cat(knitr::kable(data.frame(Outcome=unname(rd_labels[agree$outcome]),
  `Rank corr. with Medicare jump`=sprintf('%.2f',agree$rho_mcare),
  `Rank corr. with uninsured share`=sprintf('%.2f',agree$rho_uninsured),
  `Rank corr. with employment drop`=sprintf('%.2f',agree$rho_emp),
  `Minority low-ed minus white high-ed (pp)`=sprintf('%s [%s, %s]',pct(agree$diff),pct(agree$diff_lo),pct(agree$diff_hi)),
  `p-value`=pv(agree$diff_p),check.names=FALSE),align='lrrrrr',row.names=FALSE),sep='\n')
```

<div class="finding">

For doctor visits, the minority low-education minus White high-education difference is **`r pct(agree$diff[1])` pp** (95% CI `r sprintf('[%s, %s]',pct(agree$diff_lo[1]),pct(agree$diff_hi[1]))`; p = `r pv(agree$diff_p[1])`). For hospital stays it is **`r pct(agree$diff[2])` pp** (95% CI `r sprintf('[%s, %s]',pct(agree$diff_lo[2]),pct(agree$diff_hi[2]))`; p = `r pv(agree$diff_p[2])`). These are exploratory differences in subgroup discontinuities. Rank correlations use only four estimated points and ignore uncertainty in both axes; they cannot distinguish insurance effects from retirement or other group differences.

</div>

# Conclusion

```{r robust-summary, include=FALSE}
same <- subset(est,!check %in% c('main','placebo'))
same <- merge(same,main[,c('outcome','estimate')],by='outcome',suffixes=c('','_main'))
stable <- tapply(sign(same$estimate)==sign(same$estimate_main),same$outcome,all)
sig_rob <- tapply(same$p_value<.05,same$outcome,sum)
n_rob <- tapply(same$p_value,same$outcome,length)
```

<div class="finding">

**Doctor visits.** The estimated age-65 jump is **`r pct(m1$estimate)` pp** (95% CI `r ci(m1)`; p = `r pv(m1$p_value)`), relative to a fitted rate of `r pct(m1$below_rate,1)`% below 65. The estimate is `r if(m1$p_value<.05) 'statistically significant' else 'not statistically significant'` at 5%.

**Hospital stays.** The estimated jump is **`r pct(m2$estimate)` pp** (95% CI `r ci(m2)`; p = `r pv(m2$p_value)`), relative to `r pct(m2$below_rate,1)`% below 65. This secondary-outcome estimate is `r if(m2$p_value<.05) 'statistically significant' else 'not statistically significant'` at 5% before adjustment across the two main outcome tests.

After Holm adjustment across the two main outcomes, the p-values are `r pv(m1$p_holm)` for doctor visits and `r pv(m2$p_holm)` for hospital stays. `r if(all(main$p_holm>=.05)) 'Neither rejects zero at 5% under this adjustment.' else 'The adjusted results are reported alongside the prespecified primary and secondary outcome distinction.'`

**Robustness.** Doctor-visit estimates have the main estimate's sign in `r sum(same$outcome=='sawdr' & sign(same$estimate)==sign(same$estimate_main))` of `r n_rob['sawdr']` alternative specifications; hospital estimates do so in `r sum(same$outcome=='inhosp' & sign(same$estimate)==sign(same$estimate_main))` of `r n_rob['inhosp']`. Respectively, `r sig_rob['sawdr']` and `r sig_rob['inhosp']` are significant at 5%. These correlated checks are sensitivity summaries, not independent confirmations, and the exposure-exclusion specification relies on extrapolation.

**Interpretation.** Under continuity, a well-defined eligibility policy and the maintained interference assumptions, these discontinuities may be interpreted as local eligibility ITT effects. Employment and subgroup evidence support assessment of those assumptions but do not rule out independent retirement channels. Without them, the estimates describe age-65 discontinuities rather than effects attributable solely to Medicare.

</div>

## Limitations

- **Approximate inference.** Age takes few distinct values near 65, so HC1 confidence intervals do not fully account for misfit of the age trend within cells. Clustering by age cell is not used, because clustering by the running variable does not generally protect against trend misspecification (Kolesár and Rothe, 2018).
- **Recall window and extrapolation.** Past-year utilisation includes pre-eligibility time near 65. Excluding the first year above the threshold requires extrapolation and does not identify a full-year effect or guarantee attenuation of the main estimate.
- **Local effect.** The estimate applies to people around 65 in 1992-1996, not to all ages or later years.
- **Eligibility, not enrolment.** A fuzzy RD would require additional assumptions to identify a complier enrollment effect.

write.csv(est,file.path(out,'estimation_results.csv'),row.names=FALSE)
write.csv(sg,file.path(out,'subgroup_results.csv'),row.names=FALSE)
```
